module_title: Heat Treatment and Cooling of Milk

lessons.title: Pasteurization vs. Heat Treatment for Yogurt
lessons.body:
In yogurt making, heat treatment does two jobs: it kills harmful bacteria and it changes milk proteins so they can hold water and form a thick gel. Pasteurization is a specific heat treatment that uses precise time and temperature to kill pathogens. For yogurt, we often heat milk more severely than simple pasteurization. For example, heating to 85Â°C for 30 minutes or 90Â°C for 5 minutes not only pasteurizes but also denatures whey proteins, which helps the yogurt set firm without added thickeners.

In many African settings, milk may be raw or informally pasteurized. Raw milk can carry E. coli, Salmonella, and Brucella, so you must heat it properly. A simple pasteurization for drinking milk is 63Â°C for 30 minutes (low-temp long-time) or 72Â°C for 15 seconds (high-temp short-time). But for yogurt, you need higher heat. If you only pasteurize at 72Â°C for 15 seconds, your yogurt may be thin and watery because the whey proteins are not fully denatured.

Use a reliable thermometer. A digital probe thermometer costs little and is essential. If you don't have one, you can use the 'string test': heat milk while stirring, and when it starts to steam and small bubbles form around the edge, it's near 85Â°C. But a thermometer is safer. For small-scale production, a stainless steel pot on a gas burner or charcoal stove works. Stir constantly to avoid scorching. Once you reach 85Â°C, hold it there for 30 minutes, or bring to 90Â°C and hold for 5 minutes. Then cool quickly.

Remember: heat treatment for yogurt is not just about safety; it's about texture. The higher heat causes whey proteins to unfold and bind with casein, creating a stronger gel. This means you can make thick yogurt even from milk that is not very high in fat. In Africa, where refrigeration is limited, a thicker yogurt also spoils more slowly because less water separates out. So always aim for the yogurt-specific heat treatment, not just basic pasteurization.

lessons.title: High-Temperature Short-Time (HTST) Processing
lessons.body:
HTST stands for High-Temperature Short-Time. It means heating milk to a high temperature for a very short time, usually 72Â°C to 75Â°C for 15 to 20 seconds. This is common in commercial dairies because it kills pathogens quickly and preserves more of the milk's natural flavor. But for yogurt, HTST alone is often not enough to get a thick set. You need either a higher temperature or a longer holding time to denature whey proteins.

In small-scale African yogurt production, you can adapt HTST principles without expensive equipment. For example, you can heat milk to 85Â°C for 5 minutes instead of 72Â°C for 15 seconds. That is still a 'short-time' relative to 30 minutes, but it's hotter. Or you can use a two-stage process: first pasteurize at 72Â°C for 15 seconds to kill pathogens, then heat to 90Â°C for 5 minutes to denature proteins. But that's more work. Most small producers simply heat to 85Â°C for 30 minutes or 90Â°C for 5 minutes.

If you want to simulate HTST, you need a way to heat and cool quickly. A simple method: use a large pot of water as a double boiler. Heat the milk in a smaller pot inside the water bath, stirring constantly. When the milk reaches 85Â°C, start a timer for 5 minutes. Then immediately transfer the inner pot to a basin of cold water to stop the heat. This rapid cooling is part of HTST. It prevents over-cooking and keeps the milk from developing a cooked flavor.

HTST is not just about time and temperature; it's also about flow. In a factory, milk flows continuously through a heat exchanger. In your kitchen, you can mimic that by stirring constantly so all the milk gets the same heat. Never let milk sit unstirred at high heatâit will scorch and develop off-flavors. Also, use a clean thermometer that you sanitize before and after. If you don't have a thermometer, you can't do HTST reliably. So invest in one. For a 20-liter batch, a 85Â°C for 5 minutes treatment is a good compromise: it's faster than 30 minutes and still gives good protein denaturation.

lessons.title: Denaturation of Whey Proteins and Water Binding
lessons.body:
Milk proteins are mainly casein and whey proteins. Casein forms the main structure of yogurt, but whey proteins are like little balls that float in the water. When you heat milk to 85Â°C or above, the whey proteins unfoldâthis is called denaturation. Once unfolded, they can bind with casein and with water. That means the yogurt gel becomes stronger and holds more water, so you get less whey separation (the watery layer on top).

In Africa, where milk may be transported long distances and not always refrigerated, water binding is critical. A yogurt that holds water well will have a longer shelf life and a creamier texture. If you don't heat enough, the whey proteins stay folded, and they don't bind. The result is a weak gel that leaks water. You might see a pool of yellow liquid after a few hours. That is whey, and it means your heat treatment was insufficient.

To denature whey proteins, you need to hold the milk at 85Â°C for at least 20-30 minutes, or at 90Â°C for 5-10 minutes. At 85Â°C for 30 minutes, about 80-90% of whey proteins are denatured. At 90Â°C for 5 minutes, you get similar results. But if you only heat to 72Â°C for 15 seconds, less than 10% are denatured. So for yogurt, always go higher.

You can see the effect yourself. Take two batches of milk. Heat one to 85Â°C for 30 minutes, the other to 72Â°C for 15 seconds. Cool both, add the same amount of yogurt starter, and incubate. After 6 hours, the first batch will be thick and firm; the second will be thin and watery. That difference is water binding. Also, denaturation exposes more surface area for the starter bacteria to work, so fermentation may be slightly faster. But be careful: overheating above 95Â°C can cause off-flavors and destroy some vitamins. So stick to 85-90Â°C.

lessons.title: Cooling Protocols After Heat Treatment
lessons.body:
After you heat milk for yogurt, you must cool it to the incubation temperatureâusually 42-45Â°C for most yogurt cultures. If you add starter when the milk is too hot (above 50Â°C), you will kill the bacteria. If it's too cool (below 40Â°C), fermentation will be slow or fail. So cooling is as important as heating. In Africa, where ambient temperatures can be high, cooling can be a challenge. You need a fast, reliable method.

The best method is a cold water bath. After heating, put your pot of milk into a larger basin or sink filled with cold water and ice if available. Stir the milk gently to distribute the heat. Change the water if it gets warm. Within 15-20 minutes, the milk should drop from 85Â°C to 45Â°C. If you don't have ice, use the coldest water you can get, and add salt to the waterâsalt lowers the freezing point and makes the water colder. You can also use a wet cloth wrapped around the pot and a fan to speed evaporation.

Another method is to pour the hot milk into a clean, shallow container. The larger surface area helps it cool faster. But be careful: open containers can pick up contaminants. Cover with a clean cloth or lid. Never leave milk to cool overnight at room temperatureâit may pick up wild bacteria that spoil the yogurt. Cool it within 30 minutes.

Use a thermometer to check. When the milk reaches 45Â°C, it feels warm but not hot on your wrist. If you don't have a thermometer, drip a little milk on the inside of your wrist. If it feels comfortably warm (like bathwater), it's about right. But a thermometer is more accurate. Once cooled, add your starter culture immediately and mix well. Then incubate. If you cool too slowly, the milk may sit in the danger zone (40-60Â°C) where unwanted bacteria can grow. So always cool quickly and cleanly.

lessons.title: Monitoring Heat Treatment Efficacy
lessons.body:
You can't just guess that your heat treatment worked. You need to monitor it. The simplest tool is a thermometer. A digital probe thermometer with a range up to 100Â°C is cheap and accurate. Check it in boiling water (100Â°C) and ice water (0Â°C) to make sure it reads correctly. During heating, stir and check the temperature every few minutes. For a 85Â°C for 30 minutes treatment, once you reach 85Â°C, start a timer and keep the temperature between 84Â°C and 86Â°C. If it drops, increase the heat slightly. If it goes above 90Â°C, reduce heat and stir.

Another way to monitor is the 'alcohol test' for pasteurization. Mix equal parts milk and 68% ethanol (or strong local gin) in a small bottle. If the milk curdles, it means it wasn't heated enough (raw milk curdles). If it stays smooth, pasteurization was successful. This test is used in dairy labs, but you can do it in your kitchen. However, it only tells you if you reached pasteurization, not if you denatured whey proteins. For that, you need a heat treatment that goes beyond pasteurization.

You can also monitor the effect on yogurt quality. If your yogurt sets firm and doesn't leak much whey, your heat treatment was likely good. If it's thin and watery, you probably didn't heat enough. Keep records: write down the temperature, time, and how the yogurt turned out. After a few batches, you'll know what works for your milk and equipment. In Africa, milk composition varies (cow, goat, sheep), so you may need to adjust. For example, goat milk has smaller fat globules and may need slightly higher heat or longer time.

Finally, monitor cooling. Check that the milk reaches 45Â°C before adding starter. If you add starter too hot, you'll kill it and the yogurt won't ferment. If you're unsure, use a thermometer. Don't rely on touch alone. A simple logbook helps you repeat success and avoid mistakes.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Heat-Induced Defects
lessons.body:
Even with good intentions, heat treatment can go wrong. Here are common defects and how to fix them. First, scorching: if you heat milk too fast or don't stir, it burns on the bottom. The yogurt will taste burnt and may be brown. To avoid, use a heavy-bottomed pot and stir constantly. If scorching happens, don't scrape the bottom into the milk. Discard the burnt layer and use the rest only if the flavor is not affected. Otherwise, start over.

Second, over-denaturation: heating above 95Â°C or for too long can cause off-flavors (cooked, cabbage-like) and destroy vitamins. It can also make the yogurt grainy. If you accidentally overheat, cool quickly and add starter. The yogurt may still be okay but less pleasant. Next time, use a timer and thermometer.

Third, under-heating: if you don't reach 85Â°C for enough time, whey proteins don't denature, and your yogurt will be thin and leak whey. To fix, you can't reverse it after fermentation. But you can strain the yogurt to remove whey, making it thicker (like Greek yogurt). However, that reduces yield. Better to heat properly next time.

Fourth, slow cooling: if milk cools too slowly, wild bacteria can grow, causing off-flavors or gas. Cool quickly in a water bath. If you see bubbles or a yeasty smell, discard the batch.

Fifth, temperature shock to starter: if you add starter when milk is above 50Â°C, you kill the bacteria. The yogurt won't set. Check temperature with a thermometer. If it's too hot, wait. If you already added starter and it's too hot, you may need to add more starter once cooled.

Sixth, inconsistent heat: if you heat milk in a large pot without stirring, some parts may be hotter than others. This leads to uneven protein denaturation and weak gel. Always stir. Use a double boiler if possible. In Africa, where power outages are common, a gas or charcoal stove with a water bath is reliable. Keep a backup thermometer. With practice, you'll avoid these defects and make consistent, thick yogurt.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between pasteurization and heat treatment for yogurt?
options: B) Heat treatment for yogurt aims to denature whey proteins
C) Pasteurization is only for milk sold in shops
D) Heat treatment for yogurt does not kill bacteria
quiz.explanation: Yogurt heat treatment goes beyond pasteurization to denature whey proteins, improving texture.

quiz.q: Which temperature and time is recommended for yogurt-specific heat treatment?
quiz.explanation: 85Â°C for 30 minutes effectively denatures whey proteins for a thick set.

quiz.q: Why is a thermometer important in heat treatment?
options: A) To check the color of milk
B) To ensure accurate temperature and time
quiz.explanation: A thermometer ensures you reach and hold the correct temperature for safety and texture.

quiz.q: What happens if you only pasteurize at 72Â°C for 15 seconds for yogurt?
options: A) Yogurt will be too thick
B) Yogurt may be thin and watery
D) Yogurt will ferment too fast
quiz.explanation: This low heat does not denature whey proteins, leading to a weak gel.

quiz.q: What is HTST?
options: D) Heat Treatment for Soft Texture
quiz.explanation: HTST stands for High-Temperature Short-Time, a rapid pasteurization method.

quiz.q: In small-scale production, how can you mimic HTST?
quiz.explanation: 85Â°C for 5 minutes is a short-time high-heat treatment suitable for yogurt.

quiz.q: Why is rapid cooling important after heat treatment?
options: A) To prevent over-cooking and off-flavors
quiz.explanation: Rapid cooling stops the heating process and prevents cooked flavors.

quiz.q: What is denaturation of whey proteins?
quiz.explanation: Denaturation is the unfolding of protein molecules, allowing them to bind water.

quiz.q: How does denaturation affect yogurt texture?
options: B) Makes it thicker and reduces whey separation
quiz.explanation: Denatured whey proteins bind water and strengthen the gel.

quiz.q: At what temperature do whey proteins denature significantly?
quiz.explanation: 85Â°C and above causes significant denaturation of whey proteins.

quiz.q: What is the ideal incubation temperature for yogurt after cooling?
quiz.explanation: 42-45Â°C is optimal for most yogurt starter cultures.

quiz.q: What happens if you add starter to milk at 60Â°C?
options: B) Bacteria are killed and fermentation fails
quiz.explanation: High temperature kills the starter bacteria, preventing fermentation.

quiz.q: What is a good method to cool milk quickly?
options: A) Leave it on the stove
B) Put pot in cold water bath
C) Add ice directly to milk
quiz.explanation: A cold water bath conducts heat away rapidly.

quiz.q: How can you test if milk is cooled to about 45Â°C without a thermometer?
options: A) Drip on wrist, should feel comfortably warm
quiz.explanation: Dripping on the wrist gives a rough estimate of temperature.

quiz.q: What is the alcohol test used for?
quiz.explanation: The alcohol test shows if milk was properly pasteurized (no curdling).

quiz.q: What does curdling in the alcohol test indicate?
options: B) Milk is raw or under-heated
D) Milk has too much fat
quiz.explanation: Raw or under-heated milk curdles when mixed with alcohol.

quiz.q: Why keep records of heat treatment?
options: A) To repeat success and adjust for different milks
quiz.explanation: Records help you identify what works and troubleshoot issues.

quiz.q: What defect can occur if milk is heated too fast without stirring?
quiz.explanation: Scorching happens when milk burns on the bottom due to uneven heat.

quiz.q: What is a consequence of overheating milk above 95Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Overheating causes cooked flavors and nutrient loss.

quiz.q: If yogurt is thin and leaks whey, what was likely wrong?
quiz.explanation: Under-heating fails to denature whey proteins, leading to weak gel.

quiz.q: How can you salvage thin yogurt?
quiz.explanation: Straining removes excess whey and thickens the yogurt.

quiz.q: What is a sign of slow cooling after heat treatment?
quiz.explanation: Slow cooling allows wild bacteria to grow, causing defects.

quiz.q: What should you do if you accidentally add starter to milk that is too hot?
options: B) Cool and add more starter
quiz.explanation: Cooling and adding more starter can sometimes save the batch.

quiz.q: Why is stirring important during heat treatment?
options: A) To prevent scorching and ensure even heating
quiz.explanation: Stirring distributes heat evenly and prevents burning.

quiz.q: What is a good alternative heat source for small-scale yogurt production in Africa?
options: B) Gas or charcoal stove with water bath
quiz.explanation: Gas or charcoal with a water bath provides consistent, controllable heat.

quiz.q: What does HTST stand for?
options: D) Heat Treatment for Soft Texture
quiz.explanation: HTST is High-Temperature Short-Time, a rapid pasteurization method.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of cooling milk to 45Â°C before adding starter?
options: B) To provide optimal temperature for starter bacteria
quiz.explanation: 45Â°C is ideal for yogurt bacteria to grow and ferment.

quiz.q: Which of these is a heat-induced defect?
quiz.explanation: All can result from improper heat treatment or cooling.

quiz.q: How can you prevent scorching during heating?
options: A) Use high heat and stir occasionally
B) Use heavy-bottomed pot and stir constantly
quiz.explanation: A heavy pot and constant stirring prevent burning.

quiz.q: What is the recommended holding time at 90Â°C for yogurt heat treatment?
quiz.explanation: 90Â°C for 5 minutes adequately denatures whey proteins.
